COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Chosen method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an accompanying dynamic event-study (Sun & Abraham 2021 heterogeneous-timing estimator).  

Why appropriate  
• The Clean Air Act generated discrete, plausibly exogenous county-year changes in regulatory “nonattainment” status.  
• We observe the same manufacturing plants before and after status changes and can compare them to plants in counties that remain in attainment.  
• Treatment is staggered (counties move in and out of nonattainment), and the micro panel (1967-1987 quinquennial) is long enough to evaluate pre-trends and dynamic responses.  
• Plant-, county-, and industry-level fixed effects can soak up most confounders; remaining identification comes from within-plant changes around designation switches.  

Because regulation only binds for emitters, we will implement a triple-difference DID:  
(1) across county-years (nonattainment vs. attainment),  
(2) across industries (pollution-intensive vs. clean), and  
(3) over time (before vs. after designation).  
This further guards against spurious correlation between county pollution levels and local macroeconomic conditions.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Treatict = 1 if plant i is in a pollution-intensive industry c and is located in a county that is in nonattainment for the relevant pollutant in census year t; 0 otherwise.  

Pollution-intensive industry = top quartile of the 1967 national emissions distribution for the pollutant under study (constructed from EPA’s pre-CAA emissions inventory). Results will be reported pollutant-by-pollutant and pooled with industry-specific treatment dummies.  

Control group  
A. Plants in the same pollution-intensive industries but located in attainment counties (captures industry-wide shocks).  
B. Plants in the same counties but in clean industries (absorbs county-specific shocks).  
C. Our estimating equation includes both sets simultaneously.  

Treatment timing  
The “event” is the first census after a county is declared nonattainment for a given pollutant. Because status can switch, the Sun-Abraham estimator accommodates repeated treatment spells by coding exposure length d = year – first-treatment-year.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the CAA regulations, employment, capital, and shipments in high-emitting plants in future nonattainment counties would have followed the same path as comparable plants in attainment counties.  
Plausibility: Within-county × year and industry × year fixed effects soak up most common shocks; pre-trend coefficients in the event study will be inspected.  

A2. No anticipation: Firms did not accelerate or delay investment in expectation of county status changes more than 2–3 years before designation (the monitoring data that determine status were released with a lag and were not easily forecastable in the 1970s).  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Regulation in one county does not directly change outcomes in another county except through general equilibrium forces we attempt to partial out with region × year fixed effects.  

A4. Treatment exogeneity within industry: Conditional on fixed effects and demographics, county attainment status is orthogonal to unobserved shocks that differentially hit dirty vs. clean industries. This is more credible once we differentiate by industry pollution intensity.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
T1. Endogenous attainment classification (reverse causality): High industrial activity raises ambient pollution, making the county more likely to be labeled nonattainment.  
  • Mitigation: Use triple-diff; add county-specific linear trends; control for lagged county manufacturing employment; test robustness to dropping counties that ever switch back into attainment (“one-way” design).  

T2. Selective plant relocation or entry/exit: Plants anticipating stricter rules may relocate, biasing surviving-plant estimates downward.  
  • Mitigation: (i) Include exit as an outcome in a complementary logit DID; (ii) re-weight by inverse probability of survival; (iii) show results on balanced panel and full panel with zeros for exited plants.  

T3. Concurrent state or federal programs (e.g., OSHA, energy crises) correlate with pollution status.  
  • Mitigation: Add state × year fixed effects; interact year dummies with 1970 county socioeconomic covariates; repeat analysis dropping years 1974-75 (oil embargo) and 1981-82 (recession).  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --- Libraries
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE and Sun–Abraham DID
library(lubridate)

# --- 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
manu  <- fread("manufacturing_plant_panel.csv")   # plant-year data 1967-87
att   <- fread("county_attainment_status.csv")    # county-pollutant-year
emis  <- fread("industry_emissions_1967.csv")     # 4-digit SIC emissions intensity

# --- 2. Merge & variable construction --------------------------------------
## a. tag pollution-intensive industries (top quartile)
emis[, high_emit := as.integer(
        emis_intensity > quantile(emis_intensity, .75, na.rm = TRUE))]
manu  <- merge(manu, emis[, .(sic4, high_emit)], by = "sic4", all.x = TRUE)

## b. Attach county-year attainment status (choose TSP for illustration)
att_tsp <- att[pollutant == "TSP", .(county_fips, year, nonattain = status)]
manu    <- merge(manu, att_tsp, by = c("county_fips", "year"), all.x = TRUE)

## c. 5-year growth rates (align to census years)
setorder(manu, plant_id, year)
manu[, `:=`(dln_emp  = log(employment) - shift(log(employment), 1L, type="lag"),
            dln_cap  = log(capital)    - shift(log(capital), 1L, type="lag"),
            dln_ship = log(shipments)  - shift(log(shipments),1L, type="lag")),
     by = plant_id]

## d. Treatment dummy
manu[, treat := high_emit * nonattain]

## e. Event-time for Sun-Abraham (first exposure)
manu[, first_treat_year := min(year[nonattain==1]), by = county_fips]
manu[, rel_year := year - first_treat_year]            # may be NA
manu[, cohort   := fifelse(!is.na(first_treat_year), first_treat_year, 9999)]

# --- 3. Main specification --------------------------------------------------
spec_emp <- feols(dln_emp ~ sunab(cohort, rel_year, high_emit) | 
                    plant_id + county_fips^year + sic4^year,
                  data = manu[year >= 1972 & year <= 1987],
                  cluster = ~county_fips)

# --- 4. Robustness: Drop counties that switch more than once ---------------
multi_switch <- manu[, .N, by = .(county_fips, nonattain)][, 
                      times := .N, by = county_fips][times > 2, unique(county_fips)]
manu_rb <- manu[!county_fips %in% multi_switch]

spec_emp_rb <- update(spec_emp, data = manu_rb)

# --- 5. Output -------------------------------------------------------------
etable(list(Main = spec_emp, NoMultiSwitch = spec_emp_rb),
       digits = 3)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic logic suggests stricter regulation raises marginal costs of production for pollution-intensive plants, depressing employment and shipments and (depending on compliance capital) potentially raising measured capital stock. My priors (annualized % change):  
• Employment: −1.5 to −2.5 pp relative to dirty plants in attainment counties.  
• Value of shipments: −2 pp.  
• Capital: +0 to +1 pp (abatement equipment).  
Aggregated to the whole manufacturing sector the effect should be attenuated by the share of dirty plants (≈15-20 %), so roughly −0.3 pp on sectoral employment.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1: Demonstrated parallel pre-trends (will graph) …………………… 1  
C2: No obvious spillovers across counties ……………………………… 0.5  
C3: No composition bias (addressed via exit test) …………………… 0.5  
C4: Correct timing & anticipation handled ……………………………… 1  
C5: Robust to alternative specifications (shown) …………………… 1  
Total ≈ 4.0/5  

──────────────────────────────────────────────  
End of plan
